milestones.milestone_title: Clock Truth — Time Health & Device Time Authority
milestones.summary: A sustained campaign against a single class of bug: fingerprint devices whose real-time clocks drift, jump, or fail outright, silently recording arrivals at the wrong hour. DRAIS learned to measure each batch’s own drift, show device time against server time as evidence, correct a selected group of people rather than a whole day, span the midnight boundary, and recompute from raw punches without compounding earlier corrections.
milestones.significance: Attendance is only as trustworthy as the clock that stamped it. A device running five hours fast turns an on-time arrival into a late one, and the school has no way to see why. This era made the clock itself observable and correctable — and made every correction idempotent, so fixing a mistake twice does not double the damage.
key_capabilities: Device time shown against DRAIS time for first and last punches — the missing evidence
Selective correction — fix a chosen group of people, not the entire day
Corrections span the midnight boundary, catching previous-day late-night punches
Recompute-from-raw correction — idempotent, never compounds a previous fix
ADAPTIVE_DRIFT_NO_MEMORY policy for devices with a failing RTC
Historical analysis — detect clock-jump patterns in data already stored
Manual clock correction always available, never gated on DRAIS agreeing there is a problem
architectural_changes: CORRECT_BY_DRIFT measures each batch’s own drift instead of reusing a memorised offset
Fixed an asymmetric trust bug — the "device is behind" case was unbounded
Contaminated baselines no longer mask a real drift signal
Time policy became per-device configuration rather than one global rule
business_impact: Late/absent marks reflect when a learner actually arrived, not what a failing clock claimed
A school can prove, from the record, why a mark was corrected and by how much

milestones.milestone_title: Devices as Deployment Targets — Biometric Templates
milestones.summary: Fingerprint devices stopped being isolated boxes each holding their own enrolments, and became deployment targets: templates are stored centrally and pushed in bulk to a scoped set of devices, with each device reporting its role and its template readiness (X of Y synced).
milestones.significance: Enrolling a learner once per device does not scale past one device. A school with a gate reader, a dormitory reader and an office reader had to enrol every learner three times — and had no way to tell which device was missing whom.

Device role labels and template-readiness indicators (Templates X/Y, sync state)
Closed the last unreconciled gap in the central fingerprint store
architectural_changes: Central template store treated as the source of truth; devices are replicas
Deployment scoped by class/section rather than all-or-nothing
business_impact: One enrolment reaches every reader in the school
A device missing templates is visible before it causes missed attendance

milestones.summary: Two related defects closed: a student import that could overwrite an existing enrolment, and a race in admission-number assignment that had already produced duplicate learners. The import now updates in place and never touches enrolments it did not create; admission numbers gained a uniqueness constraint, and 108 existing duplicates were merged through a self-service tool rather than by hand.
milestones.significance: A duplicated learner is worse than a missing one — fees split across two records, attendance recorded against one and reported from the other, and a report card that omits half a term. This is the failure mode that quietly corrupts every downstream number.
key_capabilities: Student import updates in place and never overrides existing enrolments
Self-service duplicate-merge tool — schools resolve their own duplicates
Admission-number uniqueness enforced at the database level
architectural_changes: Admission-unique migration + closure of the insert race that created duplicates (SP-1)
Merge is a recorded operation, not a manual database edit
business_impact: 108 duplicate learners merged; the class of bug that created them is now impossible
Imports became safe to re-run — previously a second run could damage enrolments

milestones.milestone_title: Finance Consolidation — Stages A, B and C
milestones.summary: A staged consolidation of a finance module that had grown two of several things: fee items linked to charges by a real foreign key (Stage A), an active-learner undercount fixed in the older parent-facing route (Stage B), and waivers and discounts consolidated onto a single learner_fee_adjustments table (Stage C). Fee Items gained inline scope visibility and Fee Rules gained editing.
milestones.significance: Finance disagreeing with itself is the one class of bug a school cannot absorb. Two tables holding the same concept means two different answers to "what does this learner owe", and no way to tell which is right.
key_capabilities: Fee items linked to charges by foreign key, with sync-fees deduplication
Waivers and discounts unified onto learner_fee_adjustments
Fee Items shows resolved rule scope inline, not just a count
Fee Rules supports editing existing rules rather than delete-and-recreate
architectural_changes: fee_item_id FK introduced; duplicate rows removed at the source
waivers_discounts retired in favour of learner_fee_adjustments (Stage C)
Fixed an active-learner undercount in the legacy parent fees route
business_impact: One answer to what a learner owes, from every screen that asks
Fee structures can be corrected in place instead of rebuilt

milestones.milestone_title: Resilience — First Arrival Health & the Backup Center
milestones.summary: Two independent safety nets: a per-school date-rollover resilience layer that keeps "today’s first arrival" correct across the midnight boundary and timezone edges, and a Database Backup Center producing one-click, school-scoped SQL backups to off-site storage.
milestones.significance: Everything before this made DRAIS correct. This made DRAIS recoverable — a school can take its own backup without asking anyone, and the attendance day boundary stops being a source of silent wrong answers.
key_capabilities: First Arrival Health — per-school date-rollover resilience with a visible health signal
Database Backup Center — one-click, school-scoped SQL backups to Cloudinary
architectural_changes: Date rollover computed per school rather than from server-local time
Backups scoped by tenant so one school’s export never contains another’s data
business_impact: A school owns a copy of its own data, on demand
"Today’s first arrival" is correct regardless of when the day rolls over
related_commits: v1.171.0–v1.171.4 First Arrival Health — date-rollover resilience layer
v1.172.0 Database Backup Center — school-scoped SQL backups

milestones.summary: A documentation programme built as infrastructure rather than as an afterthought: architecture decision records, a database dictionary, CONTRIBUTING, a README for every subsystem (33 of 42 folders), page blueprints explaining why a screen is shaped the way it is, and a ten-lesson Developer University curriculum — with school-facing how-to guides separated from developer material and surfaced in the sidebar.
milestones.significance: The single largest risk to DRAIS was that its reasoning lived in one head. Code shows what the system does; nothing showed why. This era wrote down the decisions, the trade-offs and the shape of each subsystem so a new engineer can become useful without an oral handover.
key_capabilities: Architecture Decision Records — decisions and their trade-offs, dated and permanent
Database dictionary and a documentation index
Subsystem READMEs across DRCE, snapshots, RBAC, control, biometric, finance, portal, devices, trash, auth and more
Page blueprints — e.g. the DRCE editor, documented as an editor rather than a form
Developer University — a ten-lesson architecture-first curriculum
School-scope how-to guides split from developer docs and shown in the sidebar
architectural_changes: Documentation lives in the repository next to the code it explains
Docs are routed and readable in-app, not a separate site to keep in sync
business_impact: DRAIS can be maintained by someone who did not build it
Schools have task-shaped guides instead of engineering documentation

milestones.summary: A protracted fight with the deployment build itself. Every deploy after a certain commit had been silently failing on an out-of-memory kill, meaning fixes were being written and never shipped. Resolution came from cutting the real footprint — lazy-loading heavy export and charting libraries, removing dead dependencies and duplicate route trees, dropping 49 prerendered doc routes, and compiling with Turbopack — rather than from repeatedly raising the heap cap.
milestones.significance: This is the most dangerous failure mode a project can have: work that appears done and is not deployed. It also produced a lasting lesson recorded in the codebase — the memory ceiling was structural, not a number to tune.
key_capabilities: /api/health reports which commit is actually serving — deployment truth, not assumption
Export and charting libraries (xlsx, jspdf, html2canvas, recharts) load on demand
architectural_changes: Compile with Turbopack — webpack OOM proved not to be heap-tunable
Dead dependencies and a duplicate route tree removed; 49 doc routes no longer prerendered
Heap cap settled empirically rather than guessed
business_impact: Deploys either succeed or fail loudly — no more silent non-shipping
Anyone can verify in one request which build a site is running
related_commits: v1.173.19–v1.173.22 Stop prerendering doc routes; compile with Turbopack
v1.173.24 Drop the force-dynamic layouts — their stated cause was wrong
v1.173.26 Report which commit is actually serving

milestones.summary: Attendance devices had been unable to reach DRAIS: ADMS traffic to /iclock was being caught by the authentication middleware and answered with a redirect to the login page, which a fingerprint reader cannot follow. Device paths were excluded from the middleware matcher and added to the non-school auth scope. In the same window, the four analytics routes that had been showing "coming soon" were built, and a finance analytics 500 traced to a single wrong column name.
milestones.significance: A device that cannot post is an attendance system that does not exist. The failure was invisible from inside the app — every human-facing page worked perfectly while the machines were being turned away at the door.
key_capabilities: Fingerprint devices post attendance and operation logs without authentication interference
Student, staff, finance and academic analytics routes render real reports
Password reset flow corrected
architectural_changes: Device paths (/iclock, /api/zk-handler) excluded from the middleware matcher — middleware runs before rewrites, so exclusion is the only correct fix
NON_SCHOOL_AUTH_PREFIXES extended to cover device ingest
Attendance analytics repointed away from tables no longer written to
business_impact: Attendance data reaches the system again — the core of the product
Four reporting areas that promised "coming soon" now deliver

v1.173.27 The four "coming soon" report routes now render

milestones.summary: A seven-phase programme moving enforcement from the interface to the server: permission checks on privileged handlers, login lockout with Control Center unlock, module entitlements enforced server-side, plan capacity limits enforced at the point of creation, a single config-driven entitlement engine replacing divergent limit logic, and warnings shown on both the school and platform sides before a limit is reached.
milestones.significance: A hidden menu item is not a permission, and a plan limit the server does not check is a suggestion. This era made what a school is entitled to and what a user may do into facts the server decides, while keeping the answers visible enough that nobody is blocked by a rule they could not see coming.
key_capabilities: Server-side permission enforcement on privileged handlers
Login lockout with escalating delay, and unlock from the Control Center
Module entitlements and plan capacity limits enforced server-side
One usage number — plan, limits and gaps visible per school
Limit warnings before the ceiling is hit, on both school and platform sides
architectural_changes: checkAnyPermission added — accepts a granular code or a granted parent code
Declarative route→module map with an explicit, reasoned list of ungated routes
A single meter registry so Control Center display and enforcement cannot diverge
Lockout anchored on users.locked_until with a recorded last-failed-login time
business_impact: Role boundaries hold at the API, not just in the menu
Plans mean something commercially — and a school sees the ceiling approaching

milestones.milestone_title: Say What You Mean — Clarity, Allocations and Working Money
milestones.summary: A campaign against ambiguity in screens that were technically correct and practically unusable: snapshot lists showing raw identifiers instead of class, term and assessment names; fee scopes listing class IDs; bill search returning admission numbers instead of learner names. Alongside it, subject allocation moved onto the staff profile, audit entries became permanently and accountably deletable, profile sessions were repaired, per-school curriculums returned, and finance gained a fee circular, printable bills and a payment button that actually records a payment.
milestones.significance: Ambiguity in a school system is not cosmetic. A bursar choosing between "12004" and "12007" is one keystroke from charging the wrong class, and a snapshot list with no class names cannot be audited at all. This era closed the gap between data being present and data being usable.
key_capabilities: Snapshots show class names, term and assessment instead of raw identifiers
Fee scopes show class names; bill search matches learner names
Assign subjects to a teacher directly from the staff profile
Permanent, recorded deletion of audit entries — a deliberate act, and itself audited
Fee circular — what each class pays and who each fee applies to
Printable and exportable bills; a working payment button with receipt generation
Per-school curriculums; profile session listing repaired
architectural_changes: Snapshot list query joins terms, academic years and result types, and extracts class names from the frozen snapshot JSON
Enrolment fan-out eliminated with a derived-table join — duplicate rows and inflated totals both traced to the same cause
Audit deletion writes a tombstone recording who deleted what and how many
pdfkit font data added to Vercel output file tracing so receipt PDFs can render at runtime
business_impact: A bursar can take a payment from the learner list — previously there was nowhere to click
Report snapshots are auditable by a human without cross-referencing IDs

milestones.milestone_title: Nexus — Asking DRAIS About Your School
milestones.summary: Nexus answers questions about a school’s own records in plain language. The model never touches the database: it chooses from a fixed catalogue of read-only lookups, the server runs the chosen one with school_id taken from the session, and the rows are handed back for the model to summarise. Provider, model and key are configuration, so any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works without a code change.
milestones.significance: The first capability in DRAIS aimed at a question nobody anticipated. Its design constraint matters more than the feature: a fixed tool whitelist and session-derived tenancy mean a prompt cannot reach another school’s data, because there is no argument through which to ask.
key_capabilities: Ask questions about learners, classes, fees, attendance and results in plain language
Provider-agnostic — key, base URL and model are settings, rotatable without a deploy
Connection test that reports what the provider actually said, and a permanent setup status line
architectural_changes: Six whitelisted read-only tools — the model never generates SQL
school_id is always taken from the session, never from model arguments
Key resolved from stored setting first, environment second; never a constant in source
Provider error messages surfaced verbatim rather than reduced to a status code
business_impact: Answers to one-off questions without building a report for each one
Setup problems are self-diagnosing — the screen says what is wrong and where the key came from
